content: Breech presentation at term is associated with complications during childbirth and an increased likelihood of requiring a caesarean section. Moxibustion, a traditional Chinese medicine technique involving the burning of a specific herb near the skin, has been proposed as a method to encourage the fetus to turn from a breech to a cephalic presentation. This technique is applied to the acupuncture point Bladder 67 (BL67), also known as Zhiyin, located at the tip of the fifth toe. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of moxibustion in changing fetal presentation from breech to cephalic, reducing the need for external cephalic version (ECV), influencing the mode of delivery, and assessing perinatal morbidity and mortality. The review also aimed to assess maternal complications, maternal satisfaction, and adverse events associated with moxibustion. For this updated review, a comprehensive search of multiple databases and trial registries was conducted up to November 2021. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing moxibustion, either alone or in combination with other techniques (e.g., acupuncture or postural methods), to a control group (no moxibustion) or other interventions in women with a singleton breech presentation. Thirteen studies involving 2181 women were included in this review, with six new trials added since the last update. Most studies employed adequate methods for random sequence generation and allocation concealment. However, blinding of participants and personnel was challenging due to the nature of the intervention. Despite this, the use of objective outcomes likely minimized the impact of the lack of blinding on the results. Most studies had minimal loss to follow-up, though some trial protocols were unavailable, and one study terminated early was deemed at high risk of bias. The meta-analysis revealed that moxibustion combined with usual care probably reduces the likelihood of non-cephalic presentation at birth (moderate-certainty evidence). However, the evidence regarding its effect on the need for ECV was very uncertain due to wide confidence intervals that included both potential benefits and harms (low-certainty evidence). Moxibustion combined with usual care likely has little to no effect on the rate of caesarean section (moderate-certainty evidence). The evidence regarding its impact on premature rupture of membranes was very uncertain due to limited data (low-certainty evidence). Moxibustion combined with usual care probably reduces the use of oxytocin during labor (moderate-certainty evidence). However, the evidence regarding its effect on cord blood pH less than 7.1 was very uncertain due to insufficient data (low-certainty evidence). Adverse events, including nausea, unpleasant odor, abdominal pain, and uterine contractions, were reported in one study, but the data were limited and of very low certainty. When moxibustion plus usual care was compared to sham moxibustion plus usual care, it was found that moxibustion probably reduces the likelihood of non-cephalic presentation at birth (moderate-certainty evidence) and likely has little to no effect on the rate of caesarean section (moderate-certainty evidence). However, no studies in this comparison reported on outcomes such as the need for ECV, premature rupture of membranes, use of oxytocin, or cord blood pH less than 7.1. When moxibustion was combined with acupuncture and usual care, there was limited evidence suggesting a reduction in non-cephalic presentation at birth and at the end of treatment. There was also limited evidence regarding its effect on the need for ECV, the rate of caesarean section, and the risk of pre-eclampsia. The certainty of the evidence for these comparisons was not assessed. In conclusion, moderate-certainty evidence suggests that moxibustion combined with usual care probably reduces the likelihood of non-cephalic presentation at birth. However, the evidence regarding its effect on the need for ECV, premature rupture of membranes, and cord blood pH less than 7.1 is very uncertain. Moxibustion combined with usual care likely has little to no effect on the rate of caesarean section but probably reduces the use of oxytocin during labor. Adverse events were poorly reported across most trials, limiting the ability to draw firm conclusions about safety.
